claim: Interoception is the perception of internal bodily signals such as heartbeat, respiration, and hunger.
source: The perception of signals arising from the body such as heartbeat, respiration, and hunger is called interoception (Craig, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to Craig, 2002

claim: Individuals differ in their interoceptive sensitivity, which is the degree to which they perceive their own bodily signals.
source: Individuals differ with regard to their interoceptive sensitivity, the degree to which they perceive their own bodily signals (Critchley and Harrison, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Critchley and Harrison, 2013

claim: Interoceptive sensitivity is related to the perception of emotions, mental health, and social cognition.
source: Interoceptive sensitivity is related to human experience and behavior, such as the perception of emotions, mental health, and social cognition (Khalsa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khalsa et al., 2018

claim: Several recent theoretical accounts have highlighted that interoceptive sensitivity plays a vital role in early development in infancy.
source: Furthermore, several recent theoretical accounts have highlighted that interoceptive sensitivity plays a vital role in early development in infancy, such as the development of the self and early social abilities (Filippetti, 2021; Fotopoulou and Tsakiris, 2017; Musculus et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Filippetti, 2021; Fotopoulou and Tsakiris, 2017; Musculus et al., 2021

claim: Infants are born with limited ability to self-regulate bodily states giving rise to interoceptive sensations such as hunger.
source: As infants are born with limited ability to self-regulate bodily states giving rise to interoceptive sensations such as hunger, they rely on interactions with their primary caregiver for co-regulation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about infant development

claim: Infants rely on interactions with their primary caregiver for co-regulation of bodily states.
source: As infants are born with limited ability to self-regulate bodily states giving rise to interoceptive sensations such as hunger, they rely on interactions with their primary caregiver for co-regulation.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about infant development

claim: Interactions with primary caregivers play an important role in shaping early development in infancy.
source: These interactions in turn play an important role in shaping early development in infancy.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about infant development

claim: The first paradigm to assess cardiac interoceptive sensitivity in infancy was introduced by Maister et al., 2017.
source: Recently, the first paradigm to assess cardiac interoceptive sensitivity in infancy was introduced (Maister et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Maister et al., 2017

claim: Most empirical investigations of interoceptive processing have focused on cardiac interoception.
source: Most empirical investigations of interoceptive processing have focused on cardiac interoception (Khalsa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Khalsa et al., 2018

claim: In adults, cardiac interoceptive perception has been investigated using paradigms in which participants are asked to count or detect their own heartbeat.
source: In adults, a large body of research has investigated cardiac interoceptive perception using paradigms in which participants are asked to count or detect their own heartbeat (Brener and Ring, 2016; Schandry, 1981).
evidence: Supported by citations to Brener and Ring, 2016; Schandry, 1981

claim: Stable and adult-like interoceptive skills can be measured in children at 4–6 years of age.
source: Using modified versions of the tasks for adult participants, studies with children have shown that stable and adult-like interoceptive skills can be measured already at 4–6 y of age (Schaan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Schaan et al., 2019

claim: Maister et al., 2017 found that 5-month-old infants looked longer at stimuli that moved asynchronously to their heartbeat compared to stimuli moving synchronously.
source: Maister et al., 2017 found that infants on average looked longer at stimuli that moved asynchronously to their heartbeat as compared to stimuli moving synchronously.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maister et al., 2017

claim: Infants' cardiac interoceptive sensitivity scores were correlated with their heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs).
source: Furthermore, infants' cardiac interoceptive sensitivity scores were correlated with their heartbeat-evoked potentials (HEPs), a neural marker of interoceptive processing (Coll et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Coll et al., 2021

claim: At 5 months of age infants show sensitivity to their own cardiac signals.
source: This study provided the first evidence that already at 5 mo of age infants show sensitivity to their own cardiac signals.
evidence: Supported by citation to Maister et al., 2017

claim: The iBEATs approach has been successfully replicated with rhesus monkeys.
source: Furthermore, this approach has also successfully been replicated with rhesus monkeys (Charbonneau et al., 2022)
evidence: Supported by citation to Charbonneau et al., 2022

claim: A recent study using an adapted experimental paradigm in 6-month-old infants has found similar results to Maister et al., 2017.
source: and a recent study using an adapted experimental paradigm in 6-mo-old infants has found similar results (Imafuku et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Imafuku et al., 2023

claim: Weijs et al., 2023 reported no evidence of cardiac interoceptive sensitivity in 5- to 7-month-old infants.
source: Recently, however, no evidence of cardiac interoceptive sensitivity in 5- to 7-mo-old infants was reported (Weijs et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Weijs et al., 2023

claim: Different interoceptive modalities are not necessarily related and might have different functions or underlying neural signatures.
source: Especially, as different interoceptive modalities are not necessarily related and might have different functions or underlying neural signatures (Allen et al., 2023; Garfinkel et al., 2016; Khalsa et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Allen et al., 2023; Garfinkel et al., 2016; Khalsa et al., 2018

claim: Heartbeat and respiration are linked functionally and anatomically.

evidence: Supported by citations to Draghici and Taylor, 2016; Garcia et al., 2013

claim: Experimental paradigms measuring sensitivity to resistance in breathing have highlighted the connection between respiratory interoception and emotional states such as anxiety.

evidence: Supported by citations to Harrison et al., 2021a; Nikolova et al., 2022; Harrison et al., 2021b

claim: Breathing constitutes a fundamental process with functional significance for self-regulation.

evidence: Supported by citations to Boyadzhieva and Kayhan, 2021; Heck et al., 2016

claim: Sensitivity to respiratory signals can be observed in children from at least 10 years of age onward.

evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholson et al., 2019

claim: In children, respiratory interoception is not correlated to cardiac interoception.
source: In children, it has been reported that respiratory interoception is not correlated to cardiac interoception (Nicholson et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nicholson et al., 2019

claim: In adults, accuracy in interoceptive domains is not related across cardiac and respiratory perception.
source: In adults, it has been found that while accuracy in interoceptive domains is not related across cardiac and respiratory perception, meta-cognitive awareness for both modalities shows a significant relation (Garfinkel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garfinkel et al., 2016

claim: In adults, meta-cognitive awareness for cardiac and respiratory perception shows a significant relation.
source: In adults, it has been found that while accuracy in interoceptive domains is not related across cardiac and respiratory perception, meta-cognitive awareness for both modalities shows a significant relation (Garfinkel et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Garfinkel et al., 2016

claim: The relationship between different interoceptive modalities has not yet been investigated in early infancy.
source: In early infancy, the relationship between different interoceptive modalities has not yet been investigated.
evidence: Based on review of existing literature

claim: Around 18 months of age explicit mirror self-recognition can be observed.
source: For instance, around 18 mo of age explicit mirror self-recognition can be observed (Amsterdam, 1972).
evidence: Supported by citation to Amsterdam, 1972

claim: Around 9 months of age, the ability to show joint attention drastically matures.
source: Moreover, around 9 mo of age, the ability to show joint attention drastically matures (Carpenter et al., 1998).
evidence: Supported by citation to Carpenter et al., 1998

source: We found that for both tasks 9-mo-old infants displayed a preference for stimuli presented synchronously with their own heartbeat (Figure 1A, N=52, Msynch = 7020.62 ms SDsynch = 3790.00 ms, Masynch = 5496.7 ms, SDasynch = 2469.34 ms, t=–2.96, p=0.005, Cohens d=0.48)

claim: 9-month-old infants displayed a preference for stimuli presented synchronously with their respiration.
source: and respiration (Figure 1B, N=56, Msynch = 6336.21 ms, SDsynch = 3017.37 ms, Masynch = 5483.77 ms, SDasynch = 2244.84 ms, t=–2.80, p=0.007, Cohens d=0.32).

claim: The results replicate the approach by Maister et al., 2017 in an older age group showing that infants are sensitive to their cardiac signals.

claim: The study provides the first evidence that infants are sensitive to their respiratory signals.

claim: Mean preferences were switched compared to the results of Maister et al., 2017 who reported a mean preference for stimuli presented asynchronously to the infants' heartbeats.

claim: At 18 months, paired t-tests did not indicate a significant mean preference for the iBEATs task.

evidence: Supported by experimental data from paired t-test

claim: At 18 months, paired t-tests did not indicate a significant mean preference for the iBREATH task.
source: and iBREATH (N=30, Msynch = 3612.95 ms SDsynch = 1879.02 ms, Masynch = 4098.71 ms, SDasynch = 2074.11 ms, t(29) = 1.09, p=.283, d=–0.25) which did not indicate a significant mean preference.

claim: Equivalence tests for 18-month-olds indicate that we do not find conclusive evidence in favor of or against a mean preference effect for the iBEATs.
source: The results of the equivalence tests indicate that we do not find conclusive evidence in favor of or against a mean preference effect in our 18-mo-old sample for both the iBEATs (t(27) = 0.71, p=0.242)

claim: Equivalence tests for 18-month-olds indicate that we do not find conclusive evidence in favor of or against a mean preference effect for the iBREATH.
source: or the iBREATH ((t(29) = 1.10, p=0.141), potentially due to the small sample size.
evidence: Supported by equivalence test results

claim: There are large individual differences in preferences for synchronous versus asynchronous trials.
source: When inspecting results from our analysis approach (e.g. Figure 1), as well as previous results (Maister et al., 2017; Weijs et al., 2023) it becomes evident that there are large individual differences in preferences (e.g. some infants prefer synchronous, some asynchronous trials).
evidence: Based on visual inspection of data in Figure 1 and comparison with previous studies

claim: Sample sizes of around 30 infants might be too small to reliably detect a mean preference effect in the version of the iBEATs task used here.
source: Overall, results from the simulation indicate that sample sizes of around 30 infants might be too small to reliably detect a mean preference effect in the version of the iBEATs task used here.
evidence: Based on simulation results reported in Appendix 2

source: Using our preregistered analysis approach, we found evidence for a group mean preference for synchronous stimuli in the iBEATs (paired Bayesian t-test; BF = 2.02, mean difference: 793.95 ms, 95% CI [108.63, 1388.69], N=53, Msynch = 6131.13 ms SDsynch = 5129.93 ms, Masynch = 5337.17 ms, SDasynch = 5044.83 ms)

claim: 3-month-old infants did not show evidence for a group mean preference in the iBREATH task.
source: but not in the iBREATH task (paired Bayesian t-test; BF = 0.23, mean difference: 502.21 ms, 95% CI [–701.49, 1600.86], N=40, Msynch = 7881.72 ms SDsynch = 7641.50 ms, Masynch = 7379.50ms, SDasynch = 7220.50 ms) at 3 mo of age.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from Bayesian paired t-test

claim: For the iBREATH at 3 months, we cannot distinguish between absence or presence of an effect at least as strong as it was present in the 9-month-old's iBREATH sample.

source: This approach allowed us to include 135 observations for the iBEATs from 125 infants

evidence: Supported by statistical comparison of models

claim: For the iBREATH, the full model does not show a statistically significant better fit compared to the null model.
source: For the iBREATH we do not find a statistically significant better fit for the full compared to the null model (p=0.091).

claim: The Bayesian information criterion (BIC) for the iBREATH full model is 15.1 smaller than the null model, giving some evidence for a better fit for the full model.

claim: For both the iBEATs and iBREATH models, there was no significant interaction between age and condition.

claim: For the iBEATs, there was a significant main effect of condition on looking time in the combined sample indicating that infants show longer looking times for stimuli presented synchronously with their heartbeat over all ages.
source: For the iBEATs, we found a significant main effect of condition on looking time in the combined sample indicating that infants show longer looking times for stimuli presented synchronously with their heartbeat over all ages (OR = 1.13, 95% CI [1.03, 1.25], t(1769)=2.541, p=0.011).

claim: For the iBREATH, there was no significant effect of condition on looking time over all ages.

claim: All samples and tasks apart from the 18-month-old iBREATH sample show a numerical preference for synchronous stimuli.

claim: Across all age groups tested, infants on average prefer stimuli presented synchronously with their own heartbeat.

claim: Evidence for respiratory interoceptive sensitivity was only found in the 9-month-old sample, but not in the 3- and 18-month-olds, or the MEGA analysis.
